title: U.S. Navy Disables Cargo Ship off Iran as Gulf Blockade Deepens Middle East Tensions
snippet: American forces targeted a Singapore-bound merchant vessel in the Gulf of Oman after it attempted to breach the ongoing naval blockade of Iranian ports, U.S. Central Command confirmed Friday.
content:
WASHINGTON — The U.S. military has disabled another commercial vessel in the Gulf of Oman as American forces continue to enforce a strict naval blockade around Iranian ports, military officials confirmed Friday.

U.S. Central Command reported that a military aircraft launched precision munitions at the stern of the Palau-flagged cargo vessel M/V Pacific Archer on Thursday after it attempted to breach the blockade. The targeted strike rendered the vessel’s propulsion system useless while leaving the civilian crew unharmed. Vessel tracking data indicated the ship had departed the Iranian port of Bandar Abbas and was bound for Singapore.

Tehran Vows Counteraction Amid Stalemate

The military action prompted an immediate response from Tehran. Rear Adm. Shahram Irani, commander of Iran’s navy, declared on state television that Iranian forces would launch operations to "not only break the naval blockade but also drive the enemy out of the region’s waters."

Separately, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed that two oil tankers attempted an unauthorized transit through the Strait of Hormuz, alleging that one vessel struck a sea mine while the other was forced to turn around. Those claims could not be independently verified.

Diplomatic Pressure and Economic Fallout

The strike comes as the Trump administration navigates a complex diplomatic landscape following months of relative stalemate in the conflict that began late last winter. While regional allies including Israel have reportedly urged Washington to increase pressure on Tehran's nuclear facilities, neighboring Gulf nations, Turkey, and Pakistan have launched intense diplomatic efforts to prevent a wider military escalation.

The U.S. blockade, originally established in April and resumed in July after brief diplomatic talks, has significantly choked maritime traffic in the region. U.S. forces have intercepted or redirected 158 merchant vessels to date, with the Pacific Archer marking the 15th ship disabled by military force since the operation began.

The ongoing maritime crisis is taking a growing toll on global commerce. Industry data from Rystad Energy shows daily oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz dropped nearly 20% in early November. UN shipping analysts warn that compounded maritime disruptions across major global waterways are driving up transport costs, lengthening voyage times, and straining supply chains worldwide.
